The brief also separately recognizes that the urn remained an issue.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Examine the complete officiant statement, the complaint's precise allegations, and the evidence concerning what property Appellee allegedly removed.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's automatic-transfer proposition is inadequately supported. An affiant may establish demands for removal, elapsed time, and surrounding conduct, but the affidavit's legal conclusion that the homeowner thereby acquired title does not itself establish Ohio abandonment law or Appellant's intent to relinquish the property. Source 50 shows that Ohio law can restrict self-help seizure of tenant property, but it does not squarely decide possession left for six years after eviction, and the record describes Barney as a homeowner rather than clearly establishing a statutory landlord-tenant relationship. The attack therefore exposes a real authority gap but overstates the force of its cited source. Appellee risks losing abandonment as an undisputed, independent ground for judgment, though the marriage, payment, and burial theories remain.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Barney demanded that Appellant remove his belongings, Appellant failed to do so for more than six years after eviction, and Barney therefore legally owned and could dispose of anything left behind. The only support identified is Barney's affidavit.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Controlling Ohio abandonment and landlord-tenant authority, the prior eviction record, the nature of Barney's relationship to Appellant, and evidence bearing on intent to abandon would settle the issue.

judge_assessments.assessment: As an abstract proposition, authentic notarization does not establish the truth of an affidavit's contents, and source 49 supports only the separate Civ.R. 56 burden point. But the supplied record does not show that Appellant advanced a content-based fraud-upon-the-court theory. The brief characterizes his challenge as concerning the notary's license, signature, format, or seal and directly answers those matters. Without the actual fraud allegation or supporting evidence, the court would not decide the hypothetical claim that truthful execution failed to defeat fraud in the contents. The source cited for this attack does not supply the missing fraud standard.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The notary was licensed on the date of execution, the affidavits contained the required formal elements, a seal was affixed, the signature was not shown to be forged, and Appellant's seal and formatting objections were immaterial.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The Appellant's actual assignment of error and briefing, together with Ohio authority defining fraud upon the court, would determine whether any content-based fraud theory was preserved.

judge_assessments.assessment: The phrase 'granted ... in part' creates some ambiguity, but it does not establish a material inconsistency. The same passage explains that the court granted summary judgment and denied the separate sanctions motion, and the brief can consistently maintain that Civ.R. 56 was satisfied as to the claims on which judgment entered. The absence of the judgment entry from the materials supplied here is not an appellate defect if the entry is in the actual record; the appellate court would consult that entry rather than infer uncertainty from the answer brief's wording. Source 49 does not support the proposed record-conflict theory. Little is gained from this attack unless the actual judgment reveals unresolved claims or grounds inconsistent with final judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The court granted Appellee's motion for summary judgment 'in part,' denied the separate sanctions request, and elsewhere describes the summary-judgment motion as well taken and satisfying Civ.R. 56.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The April 11, 2013 judgment entry and the motion's requested relief would resolve the scope and finality of the disposition.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack largely duplicates the summary-judgment challenge and supplies no authority establishing an independent right to a pretrial conference. If summary judgment was valid, no pretrial was needed; if it was invalid, reversal would follow from the Civ.R. 56 error and further case management would occur on remand. Source 49 addresses summary judgment burdens, not whether a pretrial was mandatory. The brief's assertion that docket management is wholly unreviewable is too broad, but no prejudice independent of the summary-judgment ruling is identified. The court is unlikely to reach this as a separate reversible issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Because the unopposed motion was granted and was well taken, no pretrial remained necessary, and the trial court was entitled to manage its docket efficiently.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The governing common-pleas local rule, any scheduling order, and the precise relief sought in Appellant's pretrial assignment would be needed to identify an independent procedural violation.

results.verdict: mixed and vulnerable on the core Civ.R. 56 showing, though i
results.assessment: The brief is not yet persuasive as written because its summary-judgment section mostly recites the standard and declares victory without tying specific evidence to the claim and defense elements, and it too often treats Appellant’s lack of a response as if that alone made judgment proper. Its strongest point is that it does cite record materials and offers multiple alternative grounds, so the whole brief does not collapse on a single defect. The biggest remaining weakness is the categorical entitlement theory: it asserts no legal or equitable interest without adequately addressing the legal test for marital status or explaining why the cited facts necessarily defeat every ownership or possessory claim. The burial/urn framing is helpful but not conclusive.

challenges.judge_assessment: This exposes the central defect in the response's mootness theory. Corporex addresses preservation, and Hunter and In re L.W. address academic disputes, but none of the cited authorities establishes that recording a certified quiet-title judgment constitutes execution or makes corrective appellate relief impossible. Source 25 supports only the narrower distinction that recording a deed is not what passes title; it does not itself decide the effect of recording a judgment. Still, that distinction reinforces the need for authority specifically connecting this recorder filing to mootness. The trial court's and Eighth District's descriptions of the judgment as executed do not substitute for the missing legal rule. Unless the lower appellate opinion or other Ohio authority supplies that rule, the advocate risks losing the principal and purportedly dispositive reason for declining jurisdiction.

challenges.judge_assessment: The preservation principle attributed to Corporex supports the response, and the quoted characterization of the jurisdictional memorandum does not establish that the Stovalls actually argued non-mootness. Asking a court to reach the merits despite conceding execution can be a request to overlook mootness rather than a developed challenge to mootness. See Mem. at 2. This Court need not consider arguments not raised in the jurisdictional memorandum. Corporex Dev. & Constr. Mgt., Inc. v. Shook, Inc., 2005-Ohio-5409, ¶ 5, fn. 1.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response never establishes its dispositive premise that recording a certified copy of a quiet-title judgment constitutes complete execution that makes appellate relief impossible. Its own factual account identifies only a recorder filing, not a transfer to a third party, loss of possession, or any other irreversible consequence. Ohio materials distinguish recordation from the underlying passage of title: a deed may pass title whether or not it is recorded. That distinction undermines the unexplained assumption that a recorder entry necessarily extinguishes a live title controversy.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof that recording made effective appellate relief unavailable, the asserted mootness ground—and thus the requested jurisdictional dismissal—does not follow.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response's forfeiture theory conflicts with its own description of the jurisdictional memorandum. It says the Stovalls argued that the Eighth District should have reached the merits despite execution of the judgment. That is substantively a challenge to the proposition that execution required dismissal, even if the memorandum did not use the response's preferred formulation. Moreover, Ohio mootness doctrine recognizes issue-specific exceptions rather than treating every post-judgment change as categorically dispositive.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the memorandum challenged dismissal despite the recorder filing, the Court need not treat non-mootness as wholly omitted or forfeited.

attacks_proposed.argument: The assertion that merits review could not change the outcome is unsupported. The judgment adjudicated competing claims to title, and Ohio authority recognizes that possession may depend on present ownership and that competing deeds create a genuine title dispute requiring adjudication. Because recordation does not itself determine whether title validly passed, the response does not explain why reversal of the judgment could not affect the parties' title rights.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If reversal can alter the parties' legal title, the appeal is not purely academic and the principal basis for declining jurisdiction fails.

attacks_proposed.argument: The claim that the Stovalls did not present a constitutional issue is contradicted by the response's own quotation of their fourth ground: denial of due process and lack of a fair opportunity to be heard. Whether that claim ultimately succeeds is different from whether the memorandum invoked a constitutional question.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The Court should not reject constitutional jurisdiction on the premise that no constitutional claim was presented when the response itself identifies one.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response equates the theoretical availability of discovery and briefing with a constitutionally meaningful opportunity to be heard, without addressing the Stovalls' allegation that their evidence was ignored. Authorities treating procedural opportunities as due-process protections emphasize that the opportunity must be real rather than a mere formality and may include the ability to challenge the basis of the proposed deprivation. The response supplies no procedural chronology or record analysis showing that the asserted opportunity was meaningful under the circumstances.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The bare existence of procedural mechanisms does not by itself establish that no substantial due-process question exists.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response characterizes the appeal as mere error correction while simultaneously advancing a categorical legal rule that recording a certified quiet-title judgment automatically executes the judgment and moots an appeal. Ohio authorities distinguish recordation from passage of title and separately regulate stays pending appeal. Whether a recorder filing alone forecloses appellate review is therefore a legal question about the interaction of title, execution, stays, and mootness—not merely a request to reweigh case-specific evidence.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the case presents the legal consequences of recording a quiet-title judgment during the appeal period, the response's 'nothing to decide' characterization is incomplete.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response relies on the number and length of exhibits and the existence of affidavits, but quantity and authentication do not establish substantive sufficiency. It does not identify which admissible facts establish each necessary proposition supporting fraud, invalidity of the deed, and superior title. Ohio summary-judgment analysis remains claim-specific: even where testimony is uncontested, a claim fails if the required proof is absent, and judgment is proper only when the governing legal prerequisites and absence of a genuine material dispute are demonstrated.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Unless Lender first carried the affirmative Civ.R. 56 burden on every necessary issue, the absence of opposing exhibits cannot sustain summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response improperly treats the Stovalls' lack of affidavits as independently dispositive. A nonmovant's failure to submit evidence matters only after the movant has produced legally sufficient evidence establishing entitlement to judgment. Ohio materials illustrate that uncontested proof may support one claim while another claim still fails for lack of the evidence required to establish it. Thus, silence cannot cure gaps in Lender's proof of fraud or title.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The burden cannot be shifted to the Stovalls merely because their opposition lacked exhibits; Lender's threshold evidentiary burden remains essential.

attacks_proposed.argument: The response merely repeats the trial court's conclusion that the deed was fraudulent and void; it does not supply the legal standard, identify the required elements, or connect particular admissible facts to those elements. Ohio authority recognizes that competing deeds create competing claims to present title and that recordation is not itself what passes title. A quiet-title judgment therefore requires analysis of the parties' competing title claims, not repetition of the judgment's label.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without establishing why the deed was invalid as a matter of law and why Lender held the better title, the response has not justified affirmance of the quiet-title judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The merits disposition of the due-process claim rests on the unsupported characterization that the Stovalls 'declined to meaningfully participate.' The response acknowledges that Marreitta filed an opposition and quotes the claim that valid evidence was ignored, but it does not identify what material the trial court considered, what it excluded, or why. Due-process authorities emphasize an actual opportunity to contest the basis of deprivation, not merely the nominal availability of a filing procedure.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Absent a record-based account of the process actually afforded, the response cannot establish as a matter of law that the due-process claim fails.

Still, that distinction reinforces the need for authority specifically connecting this recorder filing to mootness. The trial court's and Eighth District's descriptions of the judgment as executed do not substitute for the missing legal rule. Unless the lower appellate opinion or other Ohio authority supplies that rule, the advocate risks losing the principal and purportedly dispositive reason for declining jurisdiction.

It cites no authority establishing that this particular recording completely executed a quiet-title judgment or prevented effective appellate relief.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review Salone v. Stovall, 2025-Ohio-968, and Ohio cases addressing whether recording a quiet-title decree constitutes voluntary satisfaction or execution sufficient to moot an appeal, including whether the record can be corrected following reversal.

The judgment determined ownership, and nothing quoted in the response explains why reversal could not restore the prior title position or support correction of the county record. Sources 24 and 25 establish only general propositions about competing title claims and the distinction between title and recordation; they do not directly establish the availability of appellate relief after this judgment was recorded. It does not identify the legal or practical impediment to vacating the quiet-title judgment or correcting the recorder's records after reversal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research Ohio authority on remedies after reversal of a recorded quiet-title judgment and the statutory process for recording a vacatur or appellate mandate affecting title.

judge_assessments.assessment: The preservation principle attributed to Corporex supports the response, and the quoted characterization of the jurisdictional memorandum does not establish that the Stovalls actually argued non-mootness. Asking a court to reach the merits despite conceding execution can be a request to overlook mootness rather than a developed challenge to mootness. Source 21 discusses issue-specific exceptions in eviction litigation but does not show that any exception was invoked or applies to this quiet-title appeal. Without the actual jurisdictional memorandum, the proposed attack depends on speculation about its substance.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the Stovalls conceded satisfaction or execution, did not challenge the Eighth District's mootness holding, and instead asked for merits review. It cites Corporex for the rule that issues omitted from a jurisdictional memorandum are not considered.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The Stovalls' jurisdictional memorandum would settle whether they articulated a non-mootness theory, a recognized exception, or merely requested merits review despite execution.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack blurs the difference between mentioning due process and presenting a substantial constitutional question. The response does acknowledge the due-process allegation and then argues separately in u19 that it is neither substantial nor unsettled. Thus, although u17's statement that the Stovalls did not claim a substantial constitutional question is somewhat categorical, the brief does not proceed on the premise that no constitutional words appeared. Sources 41 and 50 concern subsidized-housing procedures and do not establish substantial constitutional jurisdiction here. The court would evaluate substance, not the label, and the brief already addresses substance.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes the Stovalls' allegation that they lacked a fair opportunity to be heard, then argues that available discovery and briefing supplied due process and that failure to use those procedures does not create a substantial constitutional question.

judge_assessments.assessment: The abstract proposition that process must be meaningful is sound, but the cited sources involve administrative protections in subsidized-housing termination proceedings and do not establish a defect in this common-pleas summary-judgment process. On the supplied record, Marreitta filed an opposition without evidentiary exhibits, AdeWe filed nothing, and no denied discovery request, excluded evidence, inadequate notice, or truncated response period is identified. The allegation that evidence was ignored is not enough by itself. The brief's answer is therefore adequate on this record, and pressing this attack without identifying the supposedly ignored evidence would weaken credibility.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the Stovalls could conduct discovery and submit briefing and evidence, that Marreitta filed a two-page response without exhibits, and that AdeWe filed no response. It characterizes the claimed deprivation as failure to use available procedures.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: A docket chronology, case-management order, any discovery motions, and Marreitta's opposition would be needed to identify an actual denial of a meaningful opportunity to respond.

judge_assessments.assessment: The proposed legal question could matter only if the appellants presented it in their jurisdictional memorandum. The response says they did not challenge mootness and raised only summary-judgment complaints. A respondent's reliance on a categorical mootness rule does not itself create an appellant's proposition of law or a public-and-great-general-interest basis for review. Sources 8 and 25 address stays and deed recordation generally, not whether this unpresented issue invokes Supreme Court jurisdiction. This court would not ordinarily manufacture the proposition for the appellants.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the Stovalls omitted any challenge to mootness and presented only case-specific objections to the trial court's summary-judgment ruling.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The jurisdictional memorandum would confirm whether the consequences of recording a quiet-title judgment were actually framed as a proposition of law.

judge_assessments.assessment: It is correct that exhibit quantity and authentication do not alone establish substantive sufficiency, but the attack incorrectly treats those as the response's only showing. The factual section identifies sworn evidence that Marreitta obtained Lender's notarized signature under false pretenses, attached the signature page to a deed she prepared, represented the transfer as a gift, and recorded it. The attack identifies no specific element that this evidence fails to support. Sources 57 and 74 illustrate general proof requirements but do not establish a gap in the fraud or quiet-title showing here. At most, the response could have organized the evidence by legal element; that drafting omission is unlikely to affect discretionary jurisdiction.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Beyond counting exhibits, the brief identifies affidavits from Lender and the notary and describes the alleged fraudulent procurement, assembly, and recording of the deed with record citations. It then states that the evidence was authenticated and sufficient under Civ.R. 56.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The summary-judgment motion, affidavits, deed, and trial court entry would be necessary to test each fraud and quiet-title element directly.

judge_assessments.assessment: The burden-shifting principle is valid, but the proposed attack does not identify an actual deficiency in Lender's initial Civ.R. 56 showing. The response affirmatively says Lender supplied sufficient authenticated evidence and describes the core facts supported by affidavits. Sources 57, 74, and 79 do not demonstrate that the evidence here omitted a required element. Accordingly, the attack is a generic statement of law rather than a record-based criticism. It would matter only after showing a concrete gap in Lender's proof.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief does not rely solely on the Stovalls' silence; it first asserts that Lender met the Rule 56 standard with authenticated affidavits and exhibits, and only then argues that the Stovalls produced nothing creating a genuine dispute.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the complete Rule 56 materials for a specific missing element or an affidavit defect before advancing this burden argument.

judge_assessments.assessment: Read in isolation, u11 merely reports the trial court's conclusion. But the response elsewhere provides a factual theory of invalidity: a signature allegedly obtained under false pretenses was attached to a deed prepared by Marreitta and recorded as a gift. The attack therefore understates the brief's factual presentation. More importantly, sources 24 and 25 do not supply the governing elements, burden of proof, or void-versus-voidable rule for a fraudulently procured deed. Without that authority or a specific missing element, the proposed attack cannot establish reversible error. The advocate could improve the merits discussion, but the omission is not presently shown to threaten the jurisdictional disposition.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief reports the judgment in u11 and, in u5, describes the alleged fraudulent procurement and assembly of the deed with record citations. It does not separately state the legal elements or discuss whether the deed was void rather than voidable.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Research Ohio law governing deeds obtained by fraud, including the applicable evidentiary standard, void-versus-voidable treatment, and requirements for quieting title.

judge_assessments.assessment: The record supplied does not substantiate the premise that valid evidence was ignored. The response acknowledges Marreitta's opposition but states that it contained no evidentiary exhibits and that AdeWe filed nothing. Sources 41 and 50 concern procedural protections in subsidized-housing matters and do not show that the trial court denied these parties an actual opportunity to contest summary judgment. Due process generally guarantees an opportunity to present a case, not a favorable assessment of unsupported assertions. Without identifying evidence tendered and improperly disregarded, this attack would not land.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that discovery and opposition procedures were available, that Marreitta's response contained no evidence, and that AdeWe did not respond. It relies on Maney for the proposition that failure to follow available procedures does not require a second opportunity.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The opposition filing and trial court docket would reveal whether any Civ.R. 56 evidence was actually submitted, excluded, or overlooked.

results.assessment: The brief is strongest in framing the lower courts’ mootness ruling as the key obstacle and in preserving the forfeiture argument that the Stovalls did not fairly develop a non-mootness challenge. Its main weakness is that it never supplies the needed rule that recording a certified quiet-title judgment itself completes execution and makes appellate relief impossible; it also does not explain why reversal could not still affect title rights or the county record. The procedural forfeiture point is weaker because the memorandum’s substance is only described, not shown. The research did not settle whether this recording alone renders the case moot or whether effective relief remains available.

results.assessment: The brief is most vulnerable where it says the appeal is moot: the record of execution before appeal and no stay helps, but it does not answer the central point that reversal of a deed-voiding, ownership-determining judgment could still change the parties’ legal rights. That is the biggest gap, and the research did not settle the effect of recording a quiet-title judgment. The forfeiture argument has some traction because the Stovalls’ memorandum may not clearly preserve justiciability, but the challenge shows it is not safe to treat mootness as unchallenged. The merits fallback is also thin: the brief relies on unrebutted submissions without fully showing entitlement to judgment on each required element.

A Pennsylvania insured address, out-of-state vehicle schedule, Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM endorsements, and absence of an Ohio endorsement are substantial circumstantial evidence of intended delivery outside Ohio, especially where the brief says plaintiffs did not dispute the point. Unless the exhibits or opposing evidence show an Ohio delivery channel or Ohio recipient, this attack is unlikely to create a genuine issue.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says both policies were issued to PS Management in Volant, Pennsylvania, were not issued for delivery in Ohio, and were delivered to a named insured in Pennsylvania. It also relies on the policy exhibits and the exclusively Pennsylvania and Florida vehicle and endorsement information.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the declarations, mailing or delivery records, broker information, affidavits, and plaintiffs' opposition for evidence identifying where the policies were intended to be delivered.

judge_assessments.assessment: This frames a contested legal question as an evidentiary failure. Whether the January 2002 renewal brought Senate Bill 97 into the contract is governed by R.C. 3937.18(E), the two-year guarantee statute, and the competing renewal precedents; it is not proved through Civ.R. 56 evidence merely by avoiding the phrase 'policies at issue.' The brief does not simply assume the answer: it discusses the December 2000 inception, the two-year period, the January 2002 renewal, Arn, Advent, St. Clair, this court's contrary Storer decision, and the certified conflict. Source 50 supplies no authority on that substantive renewal question. The renewal theory faced a genuine precedential dispute, but this proposed attack does not accurately present it. Moreover, the court would not need to resolve it if it accepts the independent out-of-state-policy ground.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief provides a separate renewal analysis, acknowledges Storer and the certified conflict, distinguishes Storer because Senate Bill 267 predated the December 2000 inception, and argues that Senate Bill 97 governed upon the January 2002 renewal.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The material research would be the controlling Eighth District and Ohio Supreme Court decisions on incorporation of Senate Bill 97 during a guarantee period beginning after Senate Bill 267, rather than additional summary-judgment authority.

judge_assessments.assessment: The word 'may' in R.C. 3937.18(E) establishes permission to incorporate statutory changes; it does not, standing alone, require a separate endorsement or notice as proof of incorporation. The authorities quoted in the brief describe the law in effect at an actual renewal as governing the scope of UM/UIM coverage and state that Senate Bill 97 could be incorporated at renewal. Source 50 addresses only the generic summary-judgment burden and does not support the proposed substantive requirement for an endorsement or notice. The serious issue was whether incorporation during this guarantee period was legally permissible under Storer and the competing cases, not whether Westport produced a document saying the statute was incorporated.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on R.C. 3937.18(E), Arn, Advent, and St. Clair for the proposition that statutory changes may govern at renewal and argues that Senate Bill 97 became incorporated when the policy renewed on January 1, 2002.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the complete renewal documents and the controlling decision resolving the Advent-Storer conflict, but an endorsement requirement would need independent authority.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is speculative on the supplied record. Westport produced the binder, the subsequent printed policies, interrogatory answers, and an affidavit explaining that no physical policy was printed for the one-month initial period. The attack identifies no disputed material term, no evidence that the binder differed from the later forms, and no authority making production of a nonexistent physical policy necessary to determine statutory UM/UIM obligations. The inception and renewal dates, rather than an unidentified original clause, drive the two-year-period analysis. Any uncertainty about original terms also does not undermine the independent out-of-state issuance and vehicle-nexus defense.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says the December 2000 coverage was evidenced by a produced binder, no physical policy was printed, the later policies were produced, and no issued policy remained withheld. It also supplies inception and renewal dates through interrogatory answers and an affidavit.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The attack would require identification of a particular missing binder term and evidence that the term could alter the statutory or renewal analysis.

judge_assessments.assessment: Westport does not rely merely on plaintiffs' failure to cite authority. It affirmatively identifies the binder, later policy forms, interrogatory answers, affidavit, production notice, policy dates, and two independent legal grounds against implied coverage. Source 50 supports the ordinary Dresher burden framework but does not show that Westport failed its initial burden here. Plaintiffs' unsupported nonproduction theory therefore is not, by itself, enough to defeat an otherwise supported motion.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says all existing coverage documents were produced, no physical December 2000 policy existed, the operative renewal policies were in the record, and R.C. 3937.18 either did not apply or did not require UM/UIM coverage. It mentions the absence of plaintiffs' authority as an additional point, not its sole basis for judgment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the actual summary-judgment exhibits and opposition only to confirm their Civ.R. 56 form and whether plaintiffs identified a specific missing material term.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief treats the named insured's Pennsylvania address and Westport's Kansas address as proof that the policies were not issued for delivery in Ohio. Those facts do not themselves establish the place of issuance or delivery. The brief quotes no delivery evidence and identifies no recipient, mailing destination, broker, or transaction record establishing where either policy was delivered. (u39-u40, u59)
challenges.why_it_matters: Because place of delivery is an express component of Westport's R.C. 3937.18 theory, an unsupported inference about delivery cannot establish that statutory inapplicability as a matter of law.

target.excerpt: Neither the Business Auto Policy nor Commercial Excess Policy issued by Westport to PS Management were issued for delivery in this state, and neither were issued with respect to any vehicle registered or principally garaged in Ohio. As a result, Ohio Revised Code Section 3937.18 is not applicable to

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest record-based attack on Westport's principal, court-specific ground. R.C. 3937.18 and the cited cases support the legal rule that the statute is inapplicable when a policy was delivered or issued for delivery outside Ohio and concerns vehicles registered or principally garaged outside Ohio. But the cited authorities do not convert the insurer's Kansas address and named insured's Pennsylvania address into conclusive proof of delivery. The brief repeatedly asserts Pennsylvania delivery, yet the passages supplied identify no affidavit, mailing record, broker evidence, policy-delivery notation, or other record proof of where delivery occurred. On summary judgment, if the exhibits themselves do not establish delivery, this is a genuine evidentiary gap. Westport risks losing its cleanest independent basis for affirmance, although the separate non-Ohio garaging evidence remains substantial.
challenges.suggested_response: The policy declarations identify Westport in Kansas and PS Management in Pennsylvania, and the covered autos listed in the Business Auto Policy were garaged in Florida and Pennsylvania. Appellants have pointed to no record evidence showing that either policy was issued for delivery in Ohio or that any covered vehicle was registered or principally garaged in Ohio. On this record, R.C. 3937.18 does not apply to these policies.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Soften the delivery point. Do not present Pennsylvania and Kansas addresses as conclusive proof of where delivery occurred; instead say the record reflects Pennsylvania and Florida garaging and no record evidence identified by appellants shows Ohio delivery.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport acknowledges that this Court had already held that a policy cannot be amended to reflect statutory changes arising during the two-year guarantee period. It further acknowledges that the asserted distinction was the subject of a certified conflict still pending before the Ohio Supreme Court. The out-of-district authorities Westport cites therefore did not make its renewal theory settled Ohio law, and the brief does not demonstrate why Storer's rule is inapplicable merely because S.B. 267, rather than S.B. 97, predated the guarantee period. (u91, u95)
challenges.why_it_matters: The acknowledged contrary decision from this Court substantially undercuts Westport's claim that it was entitled to judgment as a matter of law under S.B. 97.

target.excerpt: This Court has previously held that a policy cannot be amended to reflect statutory changes that occur during the two year guarantee period. Storer v. Sharp, Cuyahoga App. No. 86525, 2006-Ohio-1577, at P 15 (attached as Exhibit 19). Storer is distinguishable from the situation in the present case wh

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands as a serious problem with the S.B. 97 alternative theory. The brief candidly identifies Storer as an Eighth District decision stating that a policy cannot be amended for statutory changes during the two-year guarantee period and acknowledges a certified conflict pending before the Supreme Court. Arn, Advent, and St. Clair support Westport's contrary position, and Westport does offer a distinction: S.B. 267 was already effective when this guarantee period began. But on the record presented, that distinction was the very disputed legal question certified for resolution; out-of-district cases did not erase this Court's own precedent. Unless intervening controlling authority had resolved the conflict by decision time, an Eighth District panel would have substantial reason to follow Storer. Westport risks losing the S.B. 97 ground for affirmance, though not necessarily the independent out-of-state delivery/garaging ground.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport acknowledges that Storer addressed a contrary result, but this case is distinguishable because the policy renewed on January 1, 2002, after S.B. 97 took effect. Arn, Advent, and St. Clair hold that the law in effect at renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and that is the rule that applies here. At a minimum, the January 1, 2002 renewal took this policy outside any claim that UM/UIM coverage could still be implied as a matter of law under the earlier version of R.C. 3937.18.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Acknowledge the Storer conflict directly, then argue why this case fits the renewal cases rather than Storer. Keep the argument as an alternative ground, but do not overstate that the issue is settled if the court had not yet resolved the conflict.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport does not adequately establish that the Commercial Excess Policy was issued only with respect to the vehicles listed in the Business Auto Policy. The excess policy itself identifies no vehicles, and Westport describes it as covering both amounts above primary insurance and amounts above a retained limit for injuries for which primary insurance is not afforded. That broader retained-limit coverage is not reconciled with the assertion that the excess policy necessarily concerns only the seven autos listed in the primary policy. (u24, u40)
challenges.why_it_matters: If the excess policy has coverage independent of the scheduled primary autos, the primary policy's Pennsylvania and Florida garaging schedule alone does not resolve whether R.C. 3937.18 applies to the excess policy.

target.excerpt: Neither the Business Auto Policy nor Commercial Excess Policy issued by Westport to PS Management were issued for delivery in this state, and neither were issued with respect to any vehicle registered or principally garaged in Ohio. As a result, Ohio Revised Code Section 3937.18 is not applicable to

challenges.judge_assessment: This exposes a material gap in extending the auto-policy garaging analysis to the excess policy. The cited delivery/garaging authorities support the statutory test, but they do not establish what vehicles or risks this particular excess policy was issued with respect to. The brief says the excess policy follows the primary auto policy's terms and therefore covers only the seven scheduled vehicles, while elsewhere describing retained-limit coverage when primary insurance is unavailable. Without the operative follow-form, retained-limit, automobile-liability, and territorial provisions, the inference that the excess policy concerns only those seven autos is not established. If the policy can directly cover automobile liability above a retained limit, the scheduled-auto facts alone may not dispose of statutory applicability. Westport risks reversal as to the excess policy even if judgment on the business-auto policy stands.
challenges.suggested_response: The Commercial Excess Policy is expressly excess over the primary insurance and, by its terms as described in the record, follows the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the primary auto policy. Because the primary Business Auto Policy covers only autos garaged in Florida and Pennsylvania, the excess policy likewise does not supply a separate Ohio automobile risk that would bring it within R.C. 3937.18. Appellants identify no policy language showing that the excess policy was issued for delivery in Ohio with respect to any motor vehicle registered or principally garaged in Ohio.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the excess-policy argument tied to the policy’s follow-form relationship to the primary auto policy, but avoid implying that the absence of a vehicle schedule by itself resolves everything. If the operative excess form is not quoted, the brief should not claim more than the record shows.

challenges.opponent_argument: The conclusion that the excess policy cannot provide UM/UIM coverage absent underlying UM/UIM coverage is asserted without analysis of the excess policy's operative insuring agreement. Westport's own description says the policy pays above a retained limit for certain injuries when primary insurance does not afford coverage. The brief does not quote or analyze language excluding UM/UIM claims from that retained-limit coverage. (u20, u24)
challenges.why_it_matters: The absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage does not, on the showing made in the brief, establish the absence of an independent obligation under the excess policy; the contractual basis for affirming summary judgment is missing.

target.excerpt: The Trial Court entered summary judgment in favor of Westport on February 27, 2007. An appeal filed by plaintiffs-appellants on March 26, 2007 was dismissed by this Court on April 13, 2007 for lack of a final appealable order. On June 5, 2007 the Trial Court issued its Nunc Pro Tunc Order finding th

challenges.judge_assessment: As a standalone contractual basis for affirmance, this is underdeveloped. No cited authority supports the categorical proposition that absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage necessarily means absence of excess coverage, and the brief does not analyze the policy language that would make that true. Its own retained-limit description suggests the excess policy may respond in some circumstances where primary insurance does not. That does not itself establish UM/UIM coverage, but it defeats the unexplained syllogism that no underlying coverage automatically means no excess obligation. Westport risks losing the trial court's separate excess-policy rationale. The attack does not by itself defeat Westport's statutory arguments or prove that Press is an insured.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport has not been shown to owe UM/UIM coverage under the Commercial Excess Policy because appellants have not identified any insuring agreement, endorsement, or other policy language that creates standalone UM/UIM coverage in that layer. The record description shows only an excess policy that pays above primary insurance and, in limited circumstances, above a retained limit; it does not show an obligation to provide UM/UIM coverage where the underlying auto policy does not. Accordingly, the trial court correctly entered summary judgment on the excess policy as well.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not state the excess-policy point as a categorical rule without contract language. Instead, say appellants have not identified any provision creating standalone UM/UIM coverage in the excess policy, and that the policy is merely an excess layer over the primary auto coverage described in the record.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport equates statutory permission to incorporate a change with actual incorporation. The quoted R.C. 3937.18(E) merely states that nothing prohibits an insurer from incorporating permitted or required changes at the beginning of a policy period; it does not make every intervening amendment automatically part of every renewal. Yet the brief identifies no renewal language, endorsement, notice, or other policy provision showing that Westport actually incorporated S.B. 97 into the January 1, 2002 policy. Its conclusion therefore does not follow from the statutory text it quotes. (u63-u65, u89-u90)
challenges.why_it_matters: Without proof of actual incorporation, Westport cannot establish that S.B. 97 governed the renewed contract and cannot obtain summary judgment on that alternative theory.

target.excerpt: The Trial Court properly entered summary judgment in favor of defendant-appellee Westport in this case where the policies at issue do not offer UM/UIM coverage in the State of Ohio, and Ohio Revised Code Section 3937.18 as amended by Senate Bill 267 and Senate Bill 97 no longer requires automobile p

challenges.judge_assessment: The textual criticism is plausible but not necessarily fatal. R.C. 3937.18(E), as quoted, permits incorporation; it does not by itself say incorporation is automatic. Yet the brief relies on cases—especially Arn, Advent, and St. Clair—for the proposition that the law in effect at an actual renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage. If those cases treated renewal itself as sufficient, Westport need not identify a separate endorsement or notice. The brief also identifies a new policy period and a separately printed 2002 renewal policy. The real vulnerability is therefore the unsettled Storer conflict, addressed more directly by a2, rather than a wholly omitted factual act of incorporation. Westport could lose the S.B. 97 theory if governing precedent required affirmative policy language adopting the amendment, but this record does not establish that requirement.
challenges.suggested_response: The Westport policies were actually renewed on January 1, 2002, after S.B. 97 became effective. Under Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, the law in effect at the time of renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and R.C. 3937.18(E) permits an insurer to incorporate statutory changes at the beginning of a policy period. Accordingly, the January 1, 2002 renewal was governed by the amended version of R.C. 3937.18, and Westport was not required to offer UM/UIM coverage or obtain a rejection.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Revise this point to say that the January 1, 2002 renewal is the event that brought S.B. 97 into the policy, and rely on Arn, Advent, and St. Clair for the proposition that the law in effect at renewal governs. Do not imply that R.C. 3937.18(E) makes every statutory change automatically part of every policy without renewal.

challenges.opponent_argument: The complaint, as characterized by Westport, seeks both medical-payments benefits and UM/UIM benefits. But the appellate argument addresses only whether UM/UIM coverage arose under R.C. 3937.18, and Westport expressly states that it is not relying on policy exclusions. It supplies no separate contractual analysis disposing of the medical-payments claim while nevertheless requesting affirmance of summary judgment on the entire action. (u13, u15, u32, u102)
challenges.why_it_matters: Even complete success on Westport's statutory UM/UIM arguments would not, without further analysis, justify affirming judgment on the separately identified medical-payments claim.

target.excerpt: For the reasons stated above, appellee Westport Insurance Corporation respectfully requests that this Honorable Court overrule appellants' assignment of error and affirm the decision of the Trial Court entering summary judgment in favor of appellee, there being no genuine issues of material fact, an

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a legitimate scope concern but may not be reached on this appellate record. Westport's case statement says the complaint sought medical-payments as well as UM/UIM benefits, while the assignment of error and legal argument address only statutory UM/UIM coverage. If the appealed judgment disposed of an independent medical-payments claim and appellants preserved and argued that issue, affirmance of the entire judgment would require a contractual basis not supplied here. But an appellate court ordinarily confines review to assigned and argued error; the record excerpt does not show that appellants separately challenged medical-payments coverage. Westport risks an overbroad affirmance or remand only if that claim remained live and was properly presented on appeal.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport’s assignment of error and argument concern the trial court’s ruling on UM/UIM coverage under R.C. 3937.18. The record and authorities discussed above establish that the policies are not subject to that statute and that UM/UIM coverage cannot be implied as a matter of law. Accordingly, the trial court’s summary judgment should be affirmed on the issue presented by this appeal.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the requested affirmance to the UM/UIM ruling unless the brief can add a separate record-and-contract basis for medical payments. If the judgment truly disposed of a separate medical-payments claim, the brief needs authority and policy language for that claim; otherwise, it should not pretend the UM/UIM analysis alone resolves it.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport admits that no physical policies were printed for the initial December 2000 period and relies instead on a binder. The brief does not quote the binder's terms or demonstrate that the binder contained every term material to UM/UIM coverage, rejection, or later renewal. Production of a document labeled a binder therefore does not by itself establish that the complete operative terms of the initial coverage were produced or that they were identical to the later policies. (u25, u30)
challenges.why_it_matters: If the initial contract's terms affect the two-year guarantee-period or renewal analysis, Westport's unexplained binder does not eliminate the factual and contractual issue on summary judgment.

challenges.judge_assessment: The attack identifies an informational omission, but it overstates what Westport had to prove. Westport says no physical policy existed for the one-month initial period, that the binder evidencing that coverage was produced, and that the printed 2001 and 2002 policies were produced. The brief's principal statutory ground turns on delivery and garaging, not on proving that every initial term was identical. The initial terms matter mainly to the disputed two-year-renewal theory. A binder's failure to reproduce all later policy terms does not itself create UM/UIM coverage or a genuine issue; appellants would need evidence or authority showing that a material initial term existed and controlled. Westport risks some force in its S.B. 97 alternative if the binder or incorporation history is incomplete, but this attack does not materially undermine the independent R.C. 3937.18 ground.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellants’ complaint that an earlier policy was not produced is incorrect. Westport produced the binder evidencing the initial one-month coverage period and produced the printed policies for the subsequent renewal periods, including the policies at issue. Appellants cite no authority holding that the absence of a separately printed initial policy creates UM/UIM coverage by operation of law or prevents application of the statutes governing the renewal policy.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Use the binder point only to defeat the nonproduction argument, not to prove the terms of the initial coverage period. The brief should say the binder and later policies were produced, and appellants cite no authority that nonproduction of a separately printed one-month policy creates UM/UIM coverage by operation of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport equates statutory permission to incorporate a change with actual incorporation. The quoted R.C. 3937.18(E) merely states that nothing prohibits an insurer from incorporating permitted or required changes at the beginning of a policy period; it does not make every intervening amendment automatically part of every renewal. Yet the brief identifies no renewal language, endorsement, notice, or other policy provision showing that Westport actually incorporated S.B. 97 into the January 1, 2002 policy. Its conclusion therefore does not follow from the statutory text it quotes. (u63-u65, u89-u90)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without proof of actual incorporation, Westport cannot establish that S.B. 97 governed the renewed contract and cannot obtain summary judgment on that alternative theory.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport acknowledges that this Court had already held that a policy cannot be amended to reflect statutory changes arising during the two-year guarantee period. It further acknowledges that the asserted distinction was the subject of a certified conflict still pending before the Ohio Supreme Court. The out-of-district authorities Westport cites therefore did not make its renewal theory settled Ohio law, and the brief does not demonstrate why Storer's rule is inapplicable merely because S.B. 267, rather than S.B. 97, predated the guarantee period. (u91, u95)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The acknowledged contrary decision from this Court substantially undercuts Westport's claim that it was entitled to judgment as a matter of law under S.B. 97.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief treats the named insured's Pennsylvania address and Westport's Kansas address as proof that the policies were not issued for delivery in Ohio. Those facts do not themselves establish the place of issuance or delivery. The brief quotes no delivery evidence and identifies no recipient, mailing destination, broker, or transaction record establishing where either policy was delivered. (u39-u40, u59)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Because place of delivery is an express component of Westport's R.C. 3937.18 theory, an unsupported inference about delivery cannot establish that statutory inapplicability as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport does not adequately establish that the Commercial Excess Policy was issued only with respect to the vehicles listed in the Business Auto Policy. The excess policy itself identifies no vehicles, and Westport describes it as covering both amounts above primary insurance and amounts above a retained limit for injuries for which primary insurance is not afforded. That broader retained-limit coverage is not reconciled with the assertion that the excess policy necessarily concerns only the seven autos listed in the primary policy. (u24, u40)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the excess policy has coverage independent of the scheduled primary autos, the primary policy's Pennsylvania and Florida garaging schedule alone does not resolve whether R.C. 3937.18 applies to the excess policy.

attacks_proposed.argument: The conclusion that the excess policy cannot provide UM/UIM coverage absent underlying UM/UIM coverage is asserted without analysis of the excess policy's operative insuring agreement. Westport's own description says the policy pays above a retained limit for certain injuries when primary insurance does not afford coverage. The brief does not quote or analyze language excluding UM/UIM claims from that retained-limit coverage. (u20, u24)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage does not, on the showing made in the brief, establish the absence of an independent obligation under the excess policy; the contractual basis for affirming summary judgment is missing.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport recasts appellants' position as though they contend that nonproduction alone automatically creates UM/UIM coverage. But the brief itself describes their actual contention as that the December 2000 coverage controls the governing statutory regime and that its terms were not produced. Whether that initial coverage controls and what it contained are analytically distinct from imposing coverage merely as a discovery sanction. (u29, u31)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Showing that nonproduction is not an independent source of coverage does not answer appellants' stated argument about which contract period and statutory regime govern.

attacks_proposed.argument: Westport admits that no physical policies were printed for the initial December 2000 period and relies instead on a binder. The brief does not quote the binder's terms or demonstrate that the binder contained every term material to UM/UIM coverage, rejection, or later renewal. Production of a document labeled a binder therefore does not by itself establish that the complete operative terms of the initial coverage were produced or that they were identical to the later policies. (u25, u30)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the initial contract's terms affect the two-year guarantee-period or renewal analysis, Westport's unexplained binder does not eliminate the factual and contractual issue on summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: The complaint, as characterized by Westport, seeks both medical-payments benefits and UM/UIM benefits. But the appellate argument addresses only whether UM/UIM coverage arose under R.C. 3937.18, and Westport expressly states that it is not relying on policy exclusions. It supplies no separate contractual analysis disposing of the medical-payments claim while nevertheless requesting affirmance of summary judgment on the entire action. (u13, u15, u32, u102)
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Even complete success on Westport's statutory UM/UIM arguments would not, without further analysis, justify affirming judgment on the separately identified medical-payments claim.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest record-based attack on Westport's principal, court-specific ground. R.C. 3937.18 and the cited cases support the legal rule that the statute is inapplicable when a policy was delivered or issued for delivery outside Ohio and concerns vehicles registered or principally garaged outside Ohio. But the cited authorities do not convert the insurer's Kansas address and named insured's Pennsylvania address into conclusive proof of delivery. The brief repeatedly asserts Pennsylvania delivery, yet the passages supplied identify no affidavit, mailing record, broker evidence, policy-delivery notation, or other record proof of where delivery occurred. On summary judgment, if the exhibits themselves do not establish delivery, this is a genuine evidentiary gap. Westport risks losing its cleanest independent basis for affirmance, although the separate non-Ohio garaging evidence remains substantial.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says both policies were issued by Westport in Kansas to PS Management in Pennsylvania, were not issued for delivery in Ohio, and were delivered to a named insured in Pennsylvania. It cites the policy exhibits and shows that the scheduled autos were garaged in Pennsylvania and Florida, but does not identify separate delivery evidence in the text.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review Exhibits 3, 5, and any underwriting, broker, mailing, or delivery records to determine whether the policies themselves or summary-judgment evidence establish delivery in Pennsylvania.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands as a serious problem with the S.B. 97 alternative theory. The brief candidly identifies Storer as an Eighth District decision stating that a policy cannot be amended for statutory changes during the two-year guarantee period and acknowledges a certified conflict pending before the Supreme Court. Arn, Advent, and St. Clair support Westport's contrary position, and Westport does offer a distinction: S.B. 267 was already effective when this guarantee period began. But on the record presented, that distinction was the very disputed legal question certified for resolution; out-of-district cases did not erase this Court's own precedent. Unless intervening controlling authority had resolved the conflict by decision time, an Eighth District panel would have substantial reason to follow Storer. Westport risks losing the S.B. 97 ground for affirmance, though not necessarily the independent out-of-state delivery/garaging ground.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief cites Arn, Advent, McDaniel, and St. Clair for incorporation at renewal; distinguishes Storer because S.B. 267 predated inception of the two-year period; cites Shay as limiting the proposition that no changes can occur; and expressly notes the certified Advent/Storer conflict pending before the Ohio Supreme Court.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The decisive research is the Ohio Supreme Court's disposition of the certified conflict in Advent and any later treatment of Storer before this appeal was decided.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes a material gap in extending the auto-policy garaging analysis to the excess policy. The cited delivery/garaging authorities support the statutory test, but they do not establish what vehicles or risks this particular excess policy was issued with respect to. The brief says the excess policy follows the primary auto policy's terms and therefore covers only the seven scheduled vehicles, while elsewhere describing retained-limit coverage when primary insurance is unavailable. Without the operative follow-form, retained-limit, automobile-liability, and territorial provisions, the inference that the excess policy concerns only those seven autos is not established. If the policy can directly cover automobile liability above a retained limit, the scheduled-auto facts alone may not dispose of statutory applicability. Westport risks reversal as to the excess policy even if judgment on the business-auto policy stands.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states that the excess policy identifies no vehicles but is subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions, and limitations as the identified primary auto policy, and concludes that it therefore covers the same Pennsylvania and Florida vehicles. It also states that the excess policy pays above primary insurance and above a retained limit for certain injuries not covered by primary insurance.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Examine Exhibit 5's insuring agreement, retained-limit clause, follow-form provision, automobile exclusions, schedule of underlying insurance, and any Ohio operations endorsements.

judge_assessments.assessment: As a standalone contractual basis for affirmance, this is underdeveloped. No cited authority supports the categorical proposition that absence of underlying UM/UIM coverage necessarily means absence of excess coverage, and the brief does not analyze the policy language that would make that true. Its own retained-limit description suggests the excess policy may respond in some circumstances where primary insurance does not. That does not itself establish UM/UIM coverage, but it defeats the unexplained syllogism that no underlying coverage automatically means no excess obligation. Westport risks losing the trial court's separate excess-policy rationale. The attack does not by itself defeat Westport's statutory arguments or prove that Press is an insured.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief reports the trial court's conclusion that the excess policy need not provide UM/UIM coverage when the underlying policies do not, and states generally that the excess policy provides sums above primary insurance and above a retained limit. It does not quote or analyze the operative provisions excluding or including UM/UIM claims.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full excess-policy language and Ohio authority distinguishing follow-form excess coverage from umbrella or retained-limit coverage would settle whether an independent UM/UIM obligation is contractually possible.

judge_assessments.assessment: The textual criticism is plausible but not necessarily fatal. R.C. 3937.18(E), as quoted, permits incorporation; it does not by itself say incorporation is automatic. Yet the brief relies on cases—especially Arn, Advent, and St. Clair—for the proposition that the law in effect at an actual renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage. If those cases treated renewal itself as sufficient, Westport need not identify a separate endorsement or notice. The brief also identifies a new policy period and a separately printed 2002 renewal policy. The real vulnerability is therefore the unsettled Storer conflict, addressed more directly by a2, rather than a wholly omitted factual act of incorporation. Westport could lose the S.B. 97 theory if governing precedent required affirmative policy language adopting the amendment, but this record does not establish that requirement.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief quotes R.C. 3937.18(E), says statutory changes could be incorporated at renewal, cites Arn, Advent, McDaniel, and St. Clair, and asserts that S.B. 97 became incorporated when the policy renewed on January 1, 2002. It does not identify a specific endorsement or notice expressly adopting S.B. 97.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the cited cases' treatment of whether incorporation occurs by operation of renewal or requires an affirmative contractual change, and inspect the 2002 renewal forms for relevant language.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a legitimate scope concern but may not be reached on this appellate record. Westport's case statement says the complaint sought medical-payments as well as UM/UIM benefits, while the assignment of error and legal argument address only statutory UM/UIM coverage. If the appealed judgment disposed of an independent medical-payments claim and appellants preserved and argued that issue, affirmance of the entire judgment would require a contractual basis not supplied here. But an appellate court ordinarily confines review to assigned and argued error; the record excerpt does not show that appellants separately challenged medical-payments coverage. Westport risks an overbroad affirmance or remand only if that claim remained live and was properly presented on appeal.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges that the complaint sought medical-payments and UM/UIM benefits, but its substantive appellate analysis addresses R.C. 3937.18 and UM/UIM coverage. It states that Westport is not relying on exclusions and requests affirmance of the entire summary judgment.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the complaint, summary-judgment motions, trial-court judgment, appellants' assignments of error, and appellate briefing to determine whether a distinct medical-payments claim was adjudicated and preserved.

judge_assessments.assessment: The attack identifies an informational omission, but it overstates what Westport had to prove. Westport says no physical policy existed for the one-month initial period, that the binder evidencing that coverage was produced, and that the printed 2001 and 2002 policies were produced. The brief's principal statutory ground turns on delivery and garaging, not on proving that every initial term was identical. The initial terms matter mainly to the disputed two-year-renewal theory. A binder's failure to reproduce all later policy terms does not itself create UM/UIM coverage or a genuine issue; appellants would need evidence or authority showing that a material initial term existed and controlled. Westport risks some force in its S.B. 97 alternative if the binder or incorporation history is incomplete, but this attack does not materially undermine the independent R.C. 3937.18 ground.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief states by affidavit and discovery response that no physical policies were printed for December 1, 2000 through January 1, 2001, that a binder was issued and produced, and that all printed policies for the later periods were produced. It also says appellants supplied no authority making nonproduction a source of implied coverage.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Inspect the binder, application, incorporated forms, and the Shea affidavit to determine what terms governed the initial month and whether the binder incorporated the subsequently issued forms.

judge_assessments.assessment: This largely misreads the brief. Westport expressly recounts appellants' position that the December 2000 coverage controls the statutory regime and that S.B. 267 and S.B. 97 therefore do not apply; it then answers that position with production facts, the January 2002 policy period, and a developed renewal-law argument. The brief also separately observes that appellants cite no authority making nonproduction itself imply coverage. That characterization may be adversarial, but it does not substitute for the renewal analysis. The court would address the actual renewal issue through a1 and a2, not treat this framing complaint as an independent defect.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief describes both strands of appellants' argument: that the December 2000 coverage controls and was not produced, and that nonproduction warrants implied coverage. It responds with the binder and later policies, then separately argues that S.B. 97 was incorporated at the January 2002 renewal.

results.assessment: The brief has a workable core because it ties the policies to non-Ohio addresses and non-Ohio garaging, and that statutory ground is its cleanest path to affirmance. But it is vulnerable in three important places: it treats addresses as proof of delivery without citing actual delivery evidence; it leans on the S.B. 97 renewal theory despite the unresolved Storer conflict and only out-of-district support; and it does not fully bridge the gap between the primary auto policy and the Commercial Excess Policy’s retained-limit language. The record as summarized leaves the excess-policy contract analysis and the incorporation question underdeveloped.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief overstates lis pendens by treating the February 2008 deed as void or as conveying no rights. Its own quoted rule says a pendente lite purchaser takes subject to the final outcome and that the plaintiff takes free of the later interest only if the plaintiff is ultimately awarded rights in the property. Thus, lis pendens preserves the court’s ability to adjudicate Solomon’s claimed interest; it does not itself establish that Solomon had superior title or prevailed on specific performance. The brief’s asserted chronology likewise shows only that the deed followed filing, not that Solomon’s underlying contract claim was valid. [2]
challenges.why_it_matters: Even if lis pendens applied, it would not supply the missing merits determination that Solomon owned the superior interest, so it does not by itself defeat Mustafa’s title or establish interference.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands strongly against the brief’s claim that the deed was void or conveyed no rights. R.C. 2703.26 and the authorities quoted in the brief make a pendente lite purchaser’s interest subject to the eventual judgment; they do not adjudicate the plaintiff’s underlying interest or automatically invalidate the conveyance. The chronology appears sufficient to invoke lis pendens because the deed followed filing and service, but that only preserves Solomon’s ability to obtain relief if his contract and specific-performance claims succeed. It does not independently establish interference or superior title. Source [2] is only indirect support, but the rule is established by the statute and cases quoted in the brief itself.
challenges.suggested_response: Solomon does not contend that lis pendens adjudicates the merits of his underlying contract claim. Rather, because this action was pending when Harwood conveyed the property to Mustafa, Mustafa took subject to Solomon’s asserted rights and to the final judgment in this case. The February 4, 2008 transfer therefore could not extinguish Solomon’s pending specific-performance claim or permit Mustafa to obtain an interest superior to whatever rights Solomon ultimately establishes. The deed and the later mortgages were, at most, subordinate to the outcome of this action, and Mustafa’s actual notice of Solomon’s claim further confirms that he cannot claim the protection of an innocent purchaser.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Concede that lis pendens does not itself prove Solomon’s superior title, and reframe the point as one of subordination and preservation of Solomon’s pending claim. Use the doctrine to defeat any argument that Mustafa’s later deed cut off the court’s ability to grant relief, not to declare the deed void in the abstract.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a substantial briefing failure. The assignment challenges enforcement of contractual indemnification, yet the argument never quotes or construes the indemnity provision and does not set out the operative escrow instructions. Its own authority limits an escrow agent’s particular duties to the escrow agreement. The alleged false HUD-1 and unilateral termination could support misconduct, but the brief still must connect that conduct to a duty owed to Solomon, resulting injury, and a rule defeating or limiting indemnification. Without that analysis, the court lacks a developed basis for reversing the contractual ruling.
challenges.suggested_response: Resource’s indemnity argument fails because the operative indemnification language and the controlling escrow instructions must be read together, and the brief does not show that those provisions authorized Resource to shield itself from liability for its own misconduct. An escrow holder’s duties are defined by the escrow agreement, and Resource’s unilateral termination of the escrow and preparation of the false HUD-1 were not faithful performance of those duties. At a minimum, those acts created a genuine issue of fact as to whether Resource acted outside the escrow instructions and whether the indemnity language could be enforced to absolve Resource of liability for its own breach of fiduciary duty, negligence, and contractual duties.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Either quote the indemnity and escrow language or limit the argument to the specific escrow duties shown in the record. The brief needs to connect Resource’s conduct to a breached escrow instruction and explain why the indemnity clause cannot cover Resource’s own misconduct.

challenges.judge_assessment: This assignment is facially deficient. Calling an order potentially final does not bring it within Civ.R. 52, and a request by Harwood does not automatically preserve an error for Solomon. More fundamentally, Civ.R. 52 generally does not require findings on summary-judgment motions. The retrieved sources do not directly prove that proposition, but the text of Civ.R. 52 and the procedural character of the rulings are controlling. Unless the challenged judgment followed a qualifying bench adjudication of a declaratory claim rather than summary judgment, this assignment fails as a matter of law.
challenges.suggested_response: The trial court’s ruling finally determined the parties’ rights on the contract and related declaratory issues without findings of fact and conclusions of law adequate to permit meaningful appellate review. Because Harwood requested findings and the court declined to supply them, the basis for the ruling remains opaque. To the extent the court resolved declaratory rights or other issues requiring findings under Civ.R. 52, the matter should be remanded for findings and conclusions sufficient to permit review of the judgment entered below.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Treat Civ.R. 52 as applicable only if the record shows a qualifying declaratory-judgment or bench determination that required findings. If the challenged ruling was summary judgment, the brief should not insist on findings as a standalone reversible error.

challenges.judge_assessment: The statutory objection has force. R.C. 5303.08 requires a qualifying title or claim within its enumerated categories, quiet possession, absence of fraud or collusion, and improvements made before commencement of the adverse-title action. The brief proves possession and alleges improvements, but it does not adequately explain how an executory purchase contract or a deed held in escrow subject to unpaid conditions amounts to obtained title within the statute. Labeling the interest color of title or equitable ownership is not enough without authority applying the occupying-claimant statute to that status.
challenges.suggested_response: Solomon was not a mere trespasser or stranger to the property. He occupied the premises under a series of purchase agreements, had made lasting improvements in reliance on those agreements, and held at least a colorable claim to the property through the deed placed in escrow. Those facts, together with his quiet possession and the absence of any fraud or collusion on his part, bring his claim within the purpose of R.C. 5303.08: to prevent eviction without compensation for lasting improvements made in reliance on an asserted ownership interest. At minimum, the statute required that Solomon’s improvement claim be adjudicated before he was turned out of possession.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not overstate the occupying-claimant statute as applying simply because Solomon possessed the property and made improvements. Either supply authority that his equitable or escrow-based status qualifies as ‘obtained title,’ or narrow the point to a request for recognition of the improvement claim separate from the statute.
